chunks: And from him, from Al-Nadhr ibn Suwayd, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Suleiman ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

In the Book of Ali (peace be upon him), that a Prophet from the Prophets complained to his Lord, saying: 'O Lord! How can I judge regarding what I did not witness and did not see?' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: 'Judge between them by My Book, and add them to My Name, so make them swear by it.'
And he (peace be upon him) said: 'This is for the one for whom a clear proof cannot be established.'
ai.seo_question: How does Islamic jurisprudence handle cases where there is no clear evidence or proof?
ai.summary: This hadith, recorded in al-Kafi, establishes the prophetic precedent for using oaths (yamin) as a legal proof in the absence of definitive evidence (bayyinah), linking judicial authority directly to divine revelation. It highlights the methodological principle in Shia jurisprudence that when factual certainty is lacking, the court relies on the sworn testimony of the parties, attributing their claim to God to ensure truthfulness. This mechanism serves as a critical bridge between divine guidance and practical adjudication in Islamic courts.
